I turn large satellite archives into measurements of change, using time series analysis
and spatial data science alongside machine learning. My main focus is coastal Antarctica,
where ice, ocean and sea ice meet. Most of my work uses synthetic aperture radar (SAR),
which sends out microwave pulses and records the echoes, so it sees through cloud and the
polar night; comparing the phase of the signal between repeat images reveals surface
movements of millimetres to centimetres.

## Methods

I work with data from several radar satellites, including Sentinel-1,
the RADARSAT Constellation Mission, TerraSAR-X, Umbra and Capella. I use
them to:

- measure ice movement by tracking features between images taken at different times;
- compare the phase of the radar signal between images to detect very small ground and ice movements (interferometry, or InSAR);
- read surface conditions, such as wet or dry snow, from the strength of the radar echo.

I also process airborne lidar, combine data from different sensors, use
machine learning with satellite images, and check results against field
measurements, including GNSS. I am building collaborations and seeking funding to
develop radioglaciology (radar on the ground or from aircraft that looks into and
through ice) in New Zealand.

## Antarctica

Around the Antarctic coast, glaciers flow into the sea and form floating ice
tongues and ice shelves. My work looks at how these floating ice
features interact with the ocean and with the sea ice around them, and measures
how fast the ice moves, how it stretches and compresses, how much ice it gains or
loses, and how thick it is. My research
has shown that the Parker Ice Tongue broke off after the land-fast sea ice that
held it in place was lost, that ocean currents bend the Erebus Ice Tongue
sideways, and how quickly ice tongues in the western Ross Sea melt from below.

I am part of the team supervising a PhD project on how sea ice and the ice
shelf interact in McMurdo Sound, using GNSS, SAR and computer models.

## New Zealand and Patagonia

In New Zealand I apply the same methods to glaciers, with students, and to
rivers and forests: I have mapped braided rivers, river-mouth lagoons (hāpua)
and forest carbon.

In Patagonia I co-authored the [first record of sea ice in the Cordillera Darwin
fjords](publications.qmd#ref-salame2020seaice) of southern Chile (Salame et al., 2020). I
also co-wrote two 2019 book chapters on fjords, in Chile and around the world. Both grew out
of my years at the CEQUA research centre in Chile (2014–2018).
